questions.stem: Population geneticists study gene pools. Which description of a gene pool is correct?
options: The set of chromosomes passed from a parent to a child
The genes that are shared by every species on Earth
All the alleles in an interbreeding population
All the genes found in the cells of one individual person
questions.explanation: A gene pool is the total collection of alleles in a population at a given time. Studying how the frequencies of alleles in it change over time is how evolution is measured.

questions.stem: What does the allele frequency of a gene describe?
options: The number of times an allele is copied during DNA replication in one cell
The proportion of people in a population who show the dominant phenotype
The rate at which new alleles of that gene appear by mutation each generation
The share of all copies of that gene in a population that are one allele
questions.explanation: Allele frequency is the fraction of all the copies of a gene in a population that are one particular allele. It differs from the proportion of people with a phenotype, because heterozygotes carry both alleles.

questions.stem: In a population of 500 people, 320 have genotype AA, 160 have Aa and 20 have aa. What is the frequency of allele a?
questions.explanation: There are 1000 copies of the gene. Allele a is carried twice by each aa person (40 copies) and once by each Aa person (160 copies), giving 200 of 1000, which is 0.2. The value 0.04 is only the proportion of aa people.

questions.stem: A sample of 200 adults in one region includes 140 with genotype HbA HbA, 56 with HbA HbS and 4 with HbS HbS. What is the frequency of the HbS allele?
questions.explanation: There are 400 copies of the gene. The HbS allele occurs 56 times in heterozygotes and 8 times in the 4 homozygotes, giving 64 of 400, which is 0.16. Adding the 56 and 4 people and dividing by 200 counts people, not alleles, and gives 0.30.

questions.stem: Population P has an allele frequency of 0.1 for a particular allele, and population Q, living in a different region, has 0.4. Fifty years later, P is 0.1 and Q is 0.25. Which statement is best supported?
options: The gene pool of P is changing over time, while that of Q is stable
Both gene pools are stable because each allele is still present
Both gene pools are changing at the same rate in the same direction
The gene pool of Q is changing over time, while that of P is stable
questions.explanation: Comparing gene pools over time shows evolution as a change in allele frequency. Q has changed from 0.4 to 0.25, while P has stayed at 0.1. The data do not show why Q has changed.

questions.stem: Why are gene pools described as dynamic?
options: Every allele in the population mutates in each new generation
Gene pools contain only dominant alleles, which keep spreading
Allele frequencies can change from one generation to the next
Individuals can change their own alleles to suit the environment
questions.explanation: Mutation, selection, genetic drift and gene flow can all alter the proportions of alleles in a population over generations. Individuals do not change their alleles in response to the environment.

questions.stem: Malaria, cold climates and food shortages have all acted as selection pressures on humans. What is a selection pressure?
options: The choice an individual makes about which allele to pass on to its offspring
An environmental factor affecting which individuals survive and reproduce
A force inside an organism that causes useful mutations to appear when needed
The pressure on a population to grow until it fills all the available space
questions.explanation: Selection pressures, such as disease, climate, predators or food supply, favour some phenotypes over others. They do not cause mutations; they act on the variation that is already present.

questions.stem: Which summary of the process of natural selection is accurate?
options: Individuals with favourable inherited traits leave more offspring, so those alleles increase
Individuals develop new traits during their lives because they need them, then pass these to offspring
Every individual in a population has the same chance of surviving and passing on its alleles
Individuals choose the traits their offspring will have so that they suit the environment better
questions.explanation: Natural selection depends on inherited variation: phenotypes that suit the environment lead to greater survival and reproduction, so the alleles responsible become more common. Traits gained during life are not inherited.

questions.stem: One of these ideas about evolution is a misunderstanding. Which one?
options: A trait that is favourable in one environment may be harmful in another
Individuals evolve during their lives to suit their environment better
Natural selection acts on phenotypes, which are influenced by genotypes
Selection changes allele frequencies in a population over generations
questions.explanation: Populations evolve, individuals do not: an individual's alleles are fixed at fertilisation. Selection acts on phenotypes and changes allele frequencies over generations, and whether a trait is favourable depends on the environment.

questions.stem: Before antibiotics, a bacterial infection was a major cause of death among young children. In a population where antibiotics are now widely available, how would the selection pressure on alleles affecting resistance to this infection most likely change?
options: It would weaken, because children with little natural resistance now usually survive
It would strengthen, because antibiotics kill children who lack resistance alleles
It would stay the same, because medicine cannot affect the human gene pool
It would disappear, because antibiotics remove the resistance alleles from the gene pool
questions.explanation: Medical treatment allows people who would once have died to survive and reproduce, so their alleles are not selected against as strongly. Humans' control over their environment has changed the selection pressures acting on them.

questions.stem: Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by homozygosity for the HbS allele and was often fatal before modern treatment. Why does the HbS allele remain common in some regions?
options: The HbS allele is dominant, so it is expressed in everyone who inherits it
Heterozygotes resist malaria better, so they survive and pass on the allele
The HbS allele mutates back to HbA in each generation, keeping both alleles common
People who are homozygous for HbS have many more children than other people
questions.explanation: People with one HbS allele and one HbA allele have some protection against severe malaria. Where malaria is common, heterozygotes survive and reproduce more than people with two HbA alleles, so HbS is kept in the gene pool despite its harm to homozygotes.

questions.stem: The frequency of the HbS allele is high in parts of Africa where malaria has long been common, but lower among descendants of Africans who have lived for generations in places without malaria. Which explanations best account for the lower frequency?
options: Without malaria, heterozygotes gain no advantage, and gene flow adds HbA alleles
Without malaria, the HbS allele mutates more often into HbA in each new generation of children
Without malaria, the mosquitoes no longer spread the HbS allele between people in the population
Without malaria, all people with the HbS allele moved back to places where malaria is found
questions.explanation: Where malaria is absent, the heterozygote advantage disappears, so selection against HbS homozygotes slowly lowers its frequency. Interbreeding with populations that have few HbS alleles (gene flow) also dilutes it. Mosquitoes transmit the malaria parasite, not the allele.

questions.stem: A map shows that the distribution of the HbS allele overlaps closely with regions where malaria has historically been common. What does this suggest?
options: Malaria acts as a selection pressure maintaining the HbS allele
The HbS allele causes malaria in people who carry two copies of it
Malaria parasites carry the HbS allele from one population to another
The HbS allele arose in each region because people needed protection
questions.explanation: The overlap suggests that malaria is the environmental factor favouring carriers of HbS. The allele arose by chance mutation and was then maintained where it gave an advantage, not because it was needed.

questions.stem: Biologists describe some changes in a gene pool as genetic drift. What does this term mean?
options: The gradual movement of a population to a new geographic location
Random changes in allele frequency from one generation to the next
Changes in allele frequency caused by migration between populations
Changes in allele frequency caused by a selection pressure in the environment
questions.explanation: Genetic drift is a change in allele frequencies due to chance, for example which individuals happen to reproduce. It is not caused by any advantage or disadvantage of the alleles involved.

questions.stem: A small, isolated village and a large city start with the same allele frequencies for a gene with no effect on survival. Where is chance alone more likely to change those frequencies noticeably, and why?
options: The city, because more people means more random events affect the gene pool
The village, because small groups always have higher rates of mutation
The city, because gene flow into large populations adds random alleles
The village, because chance events matter more when there are few individuals
questions.explanation: In a small population, which few individuals happen to reproduce can noticeably shift allele frequencies, and an allele can be lost or fixed quickly. In a large population these random effects tend to average out.

questions.stem: What is the founder effect?
options: A few founders carry only a chance sample of alleles, so frequencies differ from the source
A new population is started by the individuals best suited to a new environment, so it adapts quickly
An original population loses alleles because its founders leave and take every rare allele with them
A new population receives alleles from many different source populations, increasing its variation
questions.explanation: When a small group founds a new population, its alleles are only a sample of the original gene pool, and rare alleles may by chance be much more common or absent. This is a form of genetic drift.

questions.stem: Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, which includes extra fingers, is rare worldwide but much more common in an Amish community in Pennsylvania descended from a small number of founding families. What best explains this?
options: The community's farming way of life caused the mutation to occur repeatedly in their children
Gene flow from surrounding populations brought the allele into the community in large amounts
One of the few founders probably carried it, and people mostly married within the group
The syndrome gave the Amish a survival advantage, so natural selection increased the allele
questions.explanation: With few founders, an allele carried by one of them can make up a large share of the new gene pool. Because the community stayed reproductively separate, little gene flow diluted it. The allele is not advantageous, so selection does not explain it.

questions.stem: A typhoon kills most people on a small island, and the few survivors happen to include a carrier of a rare recessive allele for a form of colour blindness. Generations later, this colour blindness is far more common on the island than elsewhere. What process does this illustrate?
options: Gene flow from neighbouring island populations
Mutations caused by the storm in the survivors
Genetic drift following a population bottleneck
Natural selection favouring the colour-blind allele
questions.explanation: A sudden reduction in population size, a bottleneck, leaves a random sample of the original alleles. By chance, the rare allele was carried by a survivor and became common as the population regrew. Nothing about the allele helped people survive the storm.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes genetic drift from natural selection?
options: Drift is caused by mutations, while natural selection is caused by migration
Drift changes allele frequencies by chance, whatever the alleles' effects
Drift changes allele frequencies only in large populations living in stable environments
Drift always increases the frequency of favourable alleles in a population
questions.explanation: Natural selection consistently favours alleles that improve survival and reproduction in an environment. Drift is random, so it can increase harmful or neutral alleles as easily as favourable ones, especially in small populations.

questions.stem: When migrants join a population and have children there, biologists call it gene flow. What does gene flow do?
options: It moves alleles from one population's gene pool into another's
It moves alleles between chromosomes during crossing over in meiosis
It turns the information in DNA into RNA and then into protein
It removes alleles from a population as older people die
questions.explanation: Gene flow occurs when individuals move between populations and reproduce, adding alleles to one gene pool or removing them from another. Crossing over between chromosomes is a different process.

questions.stem: A gene has only two alleles, B and b. In a population the frequency of B is 0.7. What is the frequency of b?
questions.explanation: The frequencies of all the alleles of a gene add up to 1, so b = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. The values 0.49 and 0.09 are the squares of the allele frequencies, not the frequency of b.

questions.stem: Over ten generations, the frequency of allele T in a population rises from 0.20 to 0.35. T and t are the only alleles of the gene. What happened to the frequency of t?
options: It fell from 0.80 to 0.65
It rose from 0.80 to 0.95
It fell from 0.80 to 0.45
It stayed constant at 0.80
questions.explanation: Because the two frequencies always add to 1, t was 1 − 0.20 = 0.80 and became 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. A change in one allele's frequency is matched by an opposite change in the other.

questions.stem: Some genetic diseases are much more common in certain isolated populations than in the world as a whole. What best explains this?
options: Founder effects, drift and little gene flow give each population its own allele frequencies
Each population's environment directly causes the disease alleles to appear in its children
Genetic diseases spread between people in each group in the same way as infections do
Isolated populations have no mutations, so only the diseases of their founders are present
questions.explanation: In small isolated populations, the alleles carried by founders and later chance events shape the gene pool, and little gene flow dilutes them, so particular disease alleles can become common. The environment does not cause the alleles to appear.

questions.stem: What is the usual long-term effect of high gene flow between two neighbouring human populations?
options: Each population loses all of its rare alleles to the other
Each population produces new alleles at a much higher rate
Their allele frequencies become more similar to each other
Their allele frequencies become more different from each other
questions.explanation: Gene flow mixes the two gene pools, so differences in allele frequency between them are reduced. Reducing gene flow, for example by a barrier, allows the populations to diverge.

questions.stem: A mountain range separates two groups of a population, and very few people cross it for many generations. What is the most likely effect on their gene pools?
options: Their allele frequencies must stay identical, because they began as one group
Their allele frequencies become more alike, because the barrier stops mutation
Their gene pools stop changing, because barriers prevent natural selection
Their allele frequencies may diverge, as gene flow between them is reduced
questions.explanation: With little gene flow, mutation, selection and drift act separately on each group, so differences accumulate. A barrier does not stop mutation or selection within each group.

questions.stem: How does mutation alone affect allele frequencies in a large population over a few generations?
options: It has no effect, because mutations are never passed on to offspring
It introduces new alleles but changes frequencies only very slowly
It rapidly replaces the most common alleles with new ones
It removes harmful alleles from the gene pool within a generation
questions.explanation: Mutation rates for any one gene are low, so mutation alone changes allele frequencies slowly. Its importance is in supplying new alleles, which selection, drift and gene flow then act on.

questions.stem: A rare allele is found at a frequency of 0.01 in a large population. In a neighbouring small population cut off for many generations, it is not present at all. Which processes could explain its absence?
options: Natural selection alone, because rare alleles are always harmful
Mutation alone, because small groups cannot carry rare alleles
Genetic drift or a founder effect, with no gene flow to reintroduce it
Gene flow alone, which always carries rare alleles away from small groups
questions.explanation: In a small, isolated population, a rare allele can be lost by chance, or may never have been carried by its founders, and without gene flow it cannot return. A rare allele is not necessarily harmful, so selection is not required to explain its loss.

questions.stem: In the theory of evolution by natural selection, what does struggle for existence refer to?
options: Each individual tries to change its own traits to suit its environment
Species compete only with other species, never among their own members
More young are produced than can survive, so they compete for resources
Individuals fight each other until only one member of the species is left
questions.explanation: Populations produce more offspring than the environment can support, so there is competition for food, space and mates, and many die before reproducing. Which individuals survive depends partly on their inherited traits.

questions.stem: What is a species, in the biological sense?
options: A group of organisms that look identical and live in the same area
Any group of organisms that share at least one common ancestor
A group of organisms with exactly the same alleles for every gene
A group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: The biological species concept defines a species as a group whose members can interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring and are reproductively isolated from other groups. Similar appearance alone does not define a species.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of events in speciation by geographic isolation?
options: Variation, isolation, different selection and drift, reproductive isolation
Isolation, reproductive isolation, variation, different selection and drift
Different selection and drift, variation, reproductive isolation, isolation
Reproductive isolation, variation, isolation, different selection and drift
questions.explanation: A variable population is split by a barrier, the separated groups experience different selection pressures and drift so their gene pools diverge, and eventually they can no longer interbreed even if they meet.

questions.stem: Why is isolation necessary for speciation?
options: It stops gene flow, so the separated gene pools can diverge
It creates new mutations in each group that were not present before
It ensures both groups experience exactly the same selection pressures
It allows the two groups to interbreed more often than they did before
questions.explanation: Gene flow keeps populations similar. When it is stopped, differences produced by selection, mutation and drift can build up until the groups become reproductively isolated.

questions.stem: Two populations of an animal were separated by rising sea levels thousands of years ago. When some individuals are brought together today, they mate but their offspring are all infertile. What can be concluded?
options: The populations are one species, because they were once part of the same population
They are now separate species, because they are reproductively isolated
The populations are still one species because they are able to mate successfully
The populations have not changed, because the offspring were produced normally
questions.explanation: Producing only infertile offspring shows that the two gene pools can no longer combine. By the biological species concept they are now separate species, even though mating is still possible.

questions.stem: What is differential selection in the context of speciation?
options: Individuals in one population choose different mates from those in other populations
Every population is exposed to identical selection pressures but responds differently
Selection acts on genotypes directly, so phenotypes play no part in the process
Each isolated group faces different pressures, favouring different alleles
questions.explanation: When isolated populations live in different environments, different phenotypes are favoured in each. Over time this pushes their allele frequencies in different directions, contributing to divergence.

questions.stem: A student says: 'Populations change because individuals develop the traits they need to survive.' Which correction is most accurate?
options: Variation already exists; individuals with suitable inherited traits leave more offspring
Variation is created by the environment, which changes individuals to suit conditions
Variation is not inherited, so selection acts only on what happens during an individual's life
Variation is lost each generation, and new traits appear whenever they are needed
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on inherited variation that arises randomly by mutation and is reshuffled in reproduction. Individuals do not acquire inheritable traits because they need them; instead, those with favourable traits reproduce more.

questions.stem: Which list gives the mechanisms underpinning evolution by natural selection, as described in the theory?
options: Mutation only, with no part played by competition or isolation
Inherited variation, struggle for existence, isolation and differential selection
Inherited variation, use and disuse, isolation and inheritance of acquired traits
Struggle for existence, gene therapy, isolation and random mating
questions.explanation: Variation that is inherited, overproduction and competition, isolation of populations, and selection that differs between environments together change gene pools until new species can form. Use and disuse and the inheritance of acquired traits are earlier ideas that are not supported.

questions.stem: Which observation would best indicate that a change in allele frequency in a small population was caused by genetic drift rather than natural selection?
options: The allele that increased is linked to better tolerance of the local climate
The allele that increased has no known effect on survival or reproduction
The allele that increased improves resistance to a common local disease
The allele that increased is also increasing in other populations nearby
questions.explanation: If the allele gives no advantage, its rise is best explained by chance, which has a strong effect in small populations. An allele that improves disease resistance or climate tolerance would be expected to increase by selection.
